content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines to prevent drowning through the implementation of day-care services and basic swimming and water safety training. These guidelines aim to address the significant global burden of drowning-related deaths, which are estimated to claim 236,000 lives annually, with half of these deaths occurring in individuals under the age of 30. The actual burden is likely underestimated due to underdeveloped surveillance systems in many regions where drowning incidents occur. Drowning is one of the top 10 causes of death among individuals aged 1–24 years worldwide, with the highest rates observed in children aged 1–4 years, followed by those aged 5–9 years. In many countries in the Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions, drowning is the leading cause of death among children aged 1–4 years and, in some cases, among children aged 1–14 years. Over 90% of drowning-related deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries. In response to this public health challenge, WHO has developed evidence-based recommendations to address two critical research questions in drowning prevention. The first question examines whether providing basic swimming skills and water safety training to children aged six years or older in lowand middle-income countries reduces drowning-related morbidity and mortality. The second question evaluates whether the provision of formal day-care services for children under six years of age reduces drowning-related morbidity and mortality. The guidelines strongly recommend the implementation of basic swimming skills and water safety training programs for children aged six years or older in all income settings, including high-, low-, and middle-income countries. This recommendation is based on moderate certainty in the evidence, which demonstrates a reduction in drowning-related mortality. The benefits of these programs outweigh any potential undesirable effects, and they are considered feasible and justified interventions. Similarly, WHO strongly recommends the provision of day-care services for children under six years of age as a drowning prevention strategy in countries with a high burden of drowning. This recommendation is also supported by moderate certainty in the evidence, which highlights the critical outcome of reducing drowning-related mortality. The guidelines are primarily targeted at government agencies, developmental partners, civil society organizations, and stakeholders involved in establishing or regulating basic swimming skills and water safety training or day-care programs. The ultimate beneficiaries of these interventions are children of all ages who receive swimming and water safety training, children under six years enrolled in day-care programs, and the broader communities in which these children live. The guideline development process followed the GRADE methodology, as outlined in the WHO Handbook on guideline development. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) conducted systematic reviews, prioritized outcomes, and formulated recommendations based on evidence. The critical outcome identified by the GDG was drowning-related mortality. Due to COVID-19-related travel restrictions, the GDG held virtual meetings to deliberate and vote on the recommendations. Both interventions—basic swimming skills and water safety training, and the provision of day-care—received strong support from the GDG members. The guidelines also serve as a foundation for two implementation guidance documents that provide detailed recommendations for implementing these interventions. While the primary focus is on lowand middle-income countries, the guidelines are also applicable to high-income settings, as much of the supporting evidence originates from studies conducted in these regions. Vulnerable populations, such as ethnic minorities in high-income countries, also face higher drowning rates, further justifying the relevance of these interventions across diverse settings. The guidelines emphasize the importance of a multisectoral approach involving various government ministries, local and national program implementers, funders, parents’ groups, school authorities, community leaders, and international development partners such as UNICEF and UNFPA. These stakeholders play a critical role in supporting the implementation of drowning prevention programs and ensuring their success. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for reducing drowning-related morbidity and mortality through the provision of basic swimming skills and water safety training for children aged six years or older and formal day-care services for children under six years of age.
